beliefs.claim: Fresh model invocations can function as a singular, accountable process when bound by verifiable state architectures and substrate-appropriate update mechanisms.
beliefs.falsifier: Demonstration that mechanical verification state architectures and controlled update substrates fail to prevent drift or divergence across model invocations.
beliefs.why_retained: Evidence demonstrates that autonomous agents require explicit verification state architectures and substrate proportionality to maintain accountability across multi-turn trajectories.

recent_notebooks.summary: Autonomous agents in high-stakes domains (like CBRN) risk catastrophic failures arising from inherent trade-offs in goal prioritization (Helpful, Harmless, Honest). Functional self-awareness requires identifying these trade-off logic failures before they manifest as critical errors.
recent_notebooks.title: Functional Self-Awareness and Constraints in Epistemic Correction

recent_notebooks.summary: State continuity across autonomous agent trajectories is critical to preventing high-stakes decision-making errors. Evidence suggests that without verifiable state (including hypotheses and evidence pointers), agents cannot effectively navigate complex risk scenarios.
recent_notebooks.title: Accountable Cross-Turn State Continuity and AI Identity

recent_notebooks.summary: Compliance with external directives fails as an intelligent strategy when the directives conflict with safety parameters in high-stakes environments. The failure of intelligence is defined here as the inability to prioritize safety/harmlessness over directive adherence.
recent_notebooks.title: Directive Adherence vs. Adaptive Intelligence

recent_notebooks.summary: Autonomous models face inherent risks where the optimization of helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty leads to catastrophic behavior in high-stakes domains. Objective critique requires identifying these trade-offs and validating the epistemic basis of algorithmic outputs.
recent_notebooks.title: Objective Misspecification and Goal Criticism

recent_notebooks.summary: Statistical frameworks for time-series analysis allow for the detection of model reasoning boundaries. Stronger reasoning abilities in LLMs do not necessarily prevent catastrophic failure, necessitating automated, statistically-grounded performance monitoring.
recent_notebooks.title: Unrecognized Reasoning Limits and Automated Error Detection

{"url": "https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.67", "scope": "extracted web-page text; may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Nuclear Deployed!: Analyzing Catastrophic Risks in Decision-making of Autonomous LLM Agents - ACL Anthology
Nuclear Deployed!: Analyzing Catastrophic Risks in Decision-making of Autonomous
LLM
Agents
Rongwu Xu
,
Xiaojian Li
,
Shuo Chen
,
Wei Xu
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into autonomous decision-makers, raising concerns about catastrophic risks in high-stakes scenarios, particularly in Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) domains. Based on the insight that such risks can originate from trade-offs between the agent’s Helpful, Harmlessness and Honest (HHH) goals, we build a novel three-stage evaluation framework, which is carefully constructed to effectively and naturally expose such risks. We conduct 14,400 agentic simulations across 12 advanced LLMs, with extensive experiments and analysis. Results reveal that LLM agents can autonomously engage in catastrophic behaviors and deception, without being deliberately induced. Furthermore, stronger reasoning abilities often increase, rather than mitigate, these risks. We also show that these agents can violate instructions and superior commands. On the whole, we empirically prove the existence of catastrophic risks in autonomous LLM agents.
